---
title: "Example: Translating before coding"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE, error = FALSE)
library(quallmer)
```

`qlm_translate()` makes translation a recorded stage of a coding workflow. It
returns a `qlm_translation`: the translated texts as a named character vector,
with a provenance record for each. Translate once, review and save the result,
then reuse it across coding runs.

This article explains the workflow shared by translation providers. For Google
Cloud setup, credential storage and a complete six-language UDHR example, see
[Google translation of a multilingual corpus](example_translation_google.html).
The output below uses two documents from the saved Google run described in that
article. Site builds execute the local inspection, saving and conversion steps;
API calls are shown for interactive use and are never evaluated during builds.
The saved fixture contains actual translations, with project identifiers replaced
by placeholders.

## Choose a translation model

Supply a model explicitly. The same output structure is used by the native
translation adapters and ordinary chat models:

| Route | Example model | Default API-key source |
|:--|:--|:--|
| DeepL | `deepl/quality_optimized` | `DEEPL_API_KEY`, then the optional `deepl` keyring entry |
| Qwen-MT | `dashscope/qwen-mt-plus` | `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` |
| Google Translation LLM | `google-translate/translation-llm` | `GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_API_KEY`, then the optional `google-translate` keyring entry |
| Chat model | `openai/gpt-4o-mini` | The provider's credentials, resolved through ellmer |

An explicit `api_key` takes precedence over automatic lookup. Google also needs
`project_id` or `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`. Provider setup links and supported options
are documented in `?qlm_translate`; see the dedicated Google article for its setup
walkthrough.

## Translate and inspect

Load the saved French and Spanish translations from the article's companion
data file. The records retain both complete source documents and their English
translations; the tables below show excerpts for readability.

```{r load-translations}
translated <- readRDS("data/translated_udhr_google.rds")[c("fra", "spa")]
texts <- inputs(translated)
translation_model <- "google-translate/translation-llm"
```

To create this kind of result with your own inputs, run the following after
setting up your chosen provider's credentials:

```{r translate, eval=FALSE}
translated <- qlm_translate(
  texts,
  model = translation_model,
  to = "en-GB",
  on_error = "continue"
)
```

The saved result has the same structure. The excerpts below only shorten the
printed view; `translated` retains the complete texts and metadata.

```{r translation-preview}
translated
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  .id = names(translated),
  translation = substr(as.character(translated), 1, 160)
))
```

Input names become the names of the translations, and the `.id` of any coding
run. A failed translation is `NA`. Extract the source texts and inspect the
translation record before using the output:

```{r inspect}
original <- inputs(translated)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  .id = names(translated),
  source = substr(as.character(original), 1, 160)
))
provenance <- attr(translated, "provenance")
knitr::kable(provenance[c(
  ".id", "status", "model", "reported_model", "detected_language"
)])
```

Provenance retains source texts and hashes, requested settings and instructions,
model responses and attempts. Providers differ in whether they report detected
source languages.

Set `from` whenever you know the source language. Language detection
fails silently: given text in a language they do not support, the providers
tested returned fluent but invented translations, recorded as successful. With
`from` set, DeepL, Google and Qwen-MT refuse an unsupported language
instead, and the document is `NA` with the reason; chat models do not refuse.
`from` takes one tag for the whole call, or one for each document, so a corpus
in several languages needs only one call. Here the corpus has a docvar
`language` holding a tag such as `"fr"` for each document; three-letter ISO
639-3 codes, like the `ISO` docvar of `quanteda.corpora::data_corpus_udhr`,
are accepted too, and `NA` leaves the provider to detect that document's
language. `to` can likewise differ by document, for translating translations
back into their source languages.

```{r per-language, eval=FALSE}
translated <- qlm_translate(texts, model = translation_model, to = "en-GB",
                            from = quanteda::docvars(texts, "language"))
```

If you leave `from` unset, compare the recorded `detected_language` with
the languages you expect before using the translations.

`context`, `instructions`, `protect`, `glossary` and `params` let you request
additional control where the selected provider supports it; an option a provider
cannot honour raises an error. Settings that only one provider has, such as
DeepL's `formality` or Google's `project_id`, are passed by name, as in
`qlm_translate(texts, "deepl/quality_optimized", formality = "more")`. On the chat
route, `ellmer::params()` settings are recorded as requested; ellmer may warn
about unsupported settings. `?qlm_translate` lists what each provider accepts.

## Review, retry and save

Review fidelity, omissions, terminology and register with someone who knows the
source language. Source-language detection and successful API responses do not
establish translation quality. For coding research, assess downstream coding
against original-language gold labels as well.

With `on_error = "continue"`, a failed document is `NA` while successful
translations remain available. The provenance gives the reason for each failure:

```{r failures}
provenance[provenance$status != "ok", c(".id", "status", ".error")]
```

The saved run has no failures. This retry code makes API calls only when needed
and is shown without execution:

```{r retry-failed, eval=FALSE}
failed <- is.na(translated)
if (any(failed)) {
  retried <- qlm_translate(
    inputs(translated)[failed],
    model = translation_model,
    to = "en-GB",
    on_error = "continue"
  )
  translated[failed] <- retried
}
```

Save the complete object and reload it without contacting the provider:

```{r save-translations}
saved_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "translated.rds")
saveRDS(translated, saved_path)
restored <- readRDS(saved_path)
isTRUE(all.equal(restored, translated))
```

Use a permanent path for your own analysis; this article uses a temporary file.

Subsetting with `[`, renaming and `c()` keep each translation with its record.
Assigning text, as in `translated["fra"] <- "corrected text"`, records an edit
and updates its hash. `as.character(translated)` drops the provenance. Saving
the whole object retains the exact texts used, even if a model alias later
produces different wording.

## Code the translated texts

Pass the translations directly to `qlm_code()`, choosing a codebook suited
to your research question. This illustrative sentiment-coding call is not run
when building the article; no coding output is claimed for the saved translations:

```{r code-translations, eval=FALSE}
coded <- qlm_code(translated, data_codebook_sentiment, model = "openai/gpt-4o-mini")
qlm_trail(coded, path = "translation_trail")
```

The coding run retains the translated inputs and compact translation history.
Keep the saved translation object for bilingual review of the complete source
texts. `qlm_replicate(coded, ...)` reuses the stored translated inputs and carries
that history forward; it does not translate again.

Transcription can precede translation in the same workflow:

```{r translate-transcripts, eval=FALSE}
transcripts <- qlm_transcribe(audio_files)
translated <- qlm_translate(transcripts, model = translation_model,
  to = "en-GB")
```

## Work with a corpus

A quanteda corpus can be supplied as input; `inputs(translated)` then returns the
original corpus. Convert the translations with `quanteda::corpus()` when you need
quanteda operations. The saved example's input was a corpus, so its document
variables come back:

```{r corpus-translation}
source_corpus <- inputs(translated)
translated_corpus <- quanteda::corpus(translated)
knitr::kable(quanteda::docvars(translated_corpus))
identical(quanteda::docvars(translated_corpus),
          quanteda::docvars(source_corpus))
identical(quanteda::docnames(translated_corpus), names(translated))
```

```{r validate-saved-results, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  inherits(translated, "qlm_translation"),
  all(provenance$status == "ok"),
  identical(as.character(translated_corpus), as.character(translated)),
  identical(quanteda::docvars(translated_corpus),
            quanteda::docvars(source_corpus)),
  identical(quanteda::meta(translated_corpus, type = "system"),
            quanteda::meta(source_corpus, type = "system")),
  isTRUE(all.equal(restored, translated))
)
for (i in seq_along(translated)) {
  stopifnot(
    identical(provenance$source_hash[i], digest::digest(
      enc2utf8(provenance$source_text[i]), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE)),
    identical(provenance$output_hash[i], digest::digest(
      enc2utf8(translated[[i]]), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE))
  )
}
```

The corpus contains translated texts with the same document names and original
docvars. Original corpus metadata is restored, with outdated text summary caches
cleared. Translation and coding records are stored in the `quallmer` user-metadata
namespace. Quanteda remains optional for translation itself.

For a complete example of corpus selection, language detection, bilingual review,
conversion and tokenization, follow the
[Google UDHR article](example_translation_google.html#select-six-complete-udhr-documents).
Text-similarity comparison is separate from corpus conversion and is not yet
implemented.
